text:
Recent work questions whether benchmark accuracy demonstrates meaningful sequence use. [Does It Look Sequential? (RecSys 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008) evaluates 15 datasets through interaction shuffling and finds weak sequential structure in several popular benchmarks. [Spotify Research (2026)](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) distinguishes last-item models, independently aggregated pairwise transitions, and contextualized Transformers—useful controls for separating recency, broad historical associations, and joint sequence effects. [LISRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22130) extracts semantically connected history subsets to model stable preferences; its “shortcuts” mean representative items, not evidence of harmful shortcut learning.

Suggested diagnostic design: compare original histories against equal-count recent-event removal, older-event removal, and random removal; shuffle older events while preserving the last item, then shuffle the entire history. Preserve padding conventions, candidate sets, and evaluation seeds. Measure paired validation HR@10 changes, top-10 overlap, candidate-rank shifts, and final-representation cosine distance; report each category before macro averaging. To probe repeated narrow preferences, define concentration using observable item repetition or title/description similarity, without inventing category labels or treating unobserved repeat purchases as known.

These are proposed sensitivity probes, not established causal tests. Large representation changes with stable rankings suggest changes irrelevant to the measured decision; stable rankings after shuffling suggest limited order dependence under that perturbation, not proof of popularity shortcuts. Compare attention summaries with actual component ablations or output changes: attention concentration alone cannot establish explanatory importance. Removing history also changes length and position, so include matched random-removal controls and distinguish compacted deletion from position-preserving masking. Observational histories cannot establish users’ true intent, conformity, or diversity traits.
